mekki-muskil:1-1.t: His saying, the Exalted: (اقرأ باسم ربك): the bāʾ entered upon (اسم) to indicate persistence and repetition; its like is "I took hold of the halter" (أخذت بالخطام). If you said "Read the name of your Lord" and "I took the halter", there would be nothing in the speech indicating the persistence and repetition of the action. The grammarians allowed (اقرأ يا هذا) with the hamza omitted, on the assumption that the hamza was replaced by an alif before the imperative [was formed], as He said (أتستبدلون الذي هو أدنى بالذي هو خير): the alif in (أدنى), according to a group, replaces a hamza, it being from (الدناءة) "baseness". When the imperative entered upon it, the alif [printed «اللف»] was dropped for the indeclinability. It is indeclinable (mabnī) according to the Basrans and declinable according to the Kufans.

mekki-muskil:3-3.t: His saying (وربك الأكرم): a mubtadaʾ (subject) and khabar (predicate), in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the pronoun in (اقرأ).

mekki-muskil:7-8.t:
His saying (أن رآه استغنى): (أن) is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose). The hāʾ and (استغنى) are two objects of (رأى); (رأى) in the sense of knowing takes two objects. Qunbul read, from Ibn Kathīr, (أن رأه) without an alif after the hamza, as if he dropped the final radical, as it was dropped in (حاش لله). Its dropping is reported from the Arabs: it is reported (أصاب الناس) and (أوتر أهل مكة) [Translator's note: so in the source; presumably forms with a dropped final alif are meant], so they dropped the alif because the fatḥa indicates it. It has also been said that the hamza was lightened by substitution, so two alifs met, and the second was dropped because of the meeting of two vowelless letters; then when the word became deficient, the hamza was returned to its original. It is also said that the alif was dropped only because it is vowelless and the sīn after it is vowelless, since the hāʾ is a faint letter not taken into account; and the pause was run on the wording of the continuous reading, so it was dropped in the pause as it was dropped in the continuous reading, so that they would not differ. It is also said that the alif was dropped only because the imperfect of (رأى) has been used with its middle radical dropped after throwing its vowel onto what precedes it, a usage in which it became like the original, with nothing else permissible; so they said (نرى), (ترى) and (يرى). Then the past ran on that pattern, but dropping the middle radical was not possible, since there is no vowelless letter before it onto which the vowel could be thrown; so the final radical was dropped.
His saying (أرأيت): the yāʾ [Translator's note: so in the source; the tāʾ is presumably meant] is vowelless [i.e. the letter before the pronoun], and it may never take a vowel because the nominative pronoun is attached to it. Whoever does not pronounce the hamza in (أرأيت) makes the hamza between hamza and alif; it is also said that he replaced it with an alif; the first is the original.

mekki-muskil:15-15.t: His saying (لنسفعا): this nūn is the light nūn of emphasis, which entered together with the lām of the oath. The pause on it, when what precedes it has fatḥa, is with alif; and it is dropped in the pause when what precedes it has ḍamma or kasra, and what was dropped because of it is restored. If you said (الزيدون هل يقومن يا هذا) with the light nūn and then paused on it, you would restore the wāw, which is the sign of the pronoun, and restore the nūn, which is for the nominative, and say (هل يقومون). Likewise you say to a female (هل تضربن زيدا); if you pause, you restore [printed «وددت»] the yāʾ, which is the sign of the feminine, and restore the nūn, which is the sign of the nominative, and say (هل تضربين).
